column1:
User has no internet. You run ipconfig and see IPv4 Address: 169.254.34.12. What does that MOST likely indicate?

A. DNS server outage
B. The client did not receive a DHCP lease
C. The default gateway is wrong
D. The NIC driver is corrupt
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Confirms APIPA (169.254.x.x) and shows whether DHCP is enabled on the adapter.

Why it works:
APIPA is self-assigned when the client cannot obtain a DHCP lease.

Success indicates:
DHCP Enabled = Yes and IPv4 is 169.254.x.x (no valid lease).

Failure indicates:
DHCP is not reachable (wrong VLAN/SSID/port), scope exhausted, relay missing, or DHCP disabled on the client.

Common pitfall:
Jumping to DNS troubleshooting before confirming the client has a valid lease.

Next best step:
Run `ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew`, then re-check `ipconfig /all`.

column1:
After confirming a 169.254.x.x address, what is the BEST immediate action on the client?

A. ipconfig /flushdns
B. ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
C. nslookup google.com
D. Disable and re-enable the firewall
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Forces a new DHCP request and confirms resulting lease details (gateway/DNS/DHCP server).

Why it works:
This directly tests whether the client can reach DHCP and obtain a lease.

Success indicates:
Client receives a valid IP (not 169.254), gateway and DNS populated, DHCP Server shown.

Failure indicates:
Renew fails or returns APIPA again, pointing to DHCP reachability, VLAN/SSID, scope exhaustion, or blocked DHCP traffic.

Common pitfall:
Only running /renew without checking the final lease details in ipconfig /all.

column1:
ipconfig /all shows 'DHCP Enabled: No' and the user has a bad IP configuration. What is the MOST likely issue?

A. DNS misconfiguration
B. Adapter is set to static / not set to obtain IP automatically
C. DHCP scope is exhausted
D. Router is down
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether the adapter is configured to use DHCP or static addressing.

Why it works:
If DHCP is disabled, the client won’t request a lease and may be misconfigured.

Success indicates:
After setting DHCP enabled, /renew obtains a valid lease and connectivity returns.

Failure indicates:
DHCP remains disabled or static settings remain incorrect (wrong subnet/gateway/DNS).

Common pitfall:
Assuming the DHCP server is down when the client is simply not configured to use DHCP.

column1:
Two users on the same floor: one works, one has 169.254.x.x. What is the BEST next move?

A. Reboot DHCP server
B. Compare ipconfig /all on working vs failing machines
C. Flush DNS on both machines
D. Reset both passwords
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (working)
ipconfig /all (failing)

What it checks:
IP range, gateway, DNS, DHCP Server, and adapter differences.

Why it works:
A known-good baseline reveals VLAN/SSID/port differences or rogue DHCP quickly.

Success indicates:
Working and failing configs match expected design; failing client then points to local link issue.

Failure indicates:
Failing client shows APIPA or different DHCP Server/IP range than working client.

Common pitfall:
Troubleshooting only the failing machine without comparing to a working one.

column1:
Wi‑Fi shows connected, but the client has 169.254.x.x. What is the most likely explanation?

A. Wi‑Fi auth succeeded but DHCP did not complete
B. DNS is down
C. Wrong gateway
D. Password expired
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Whether the client obtained a lease despite being associated to Wi‑Fi.

Why it works:
Association/authentication can succeed even if DHCP traffic is blocked or not available on that SSID/VLAN.

Success indicates:
After renew, client receives valid lease and can reach gateway/internet/internal resources as appropriate.

Failure indicates:
Renew fails or returns APIPA, indicating DHCP not reachable on that SSID/VLAN or scope exhausted.

Common pitfall:
Assuming 'connected' equals 'fully configured'.

column1:
Which single command gives the most complete DHCP lease picture on Windows?

A. ipconfig
B. ipconfig /all
C. ping
D. nslookup
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
IP, mask, gateway, DNS, DHCP Server, lease obtained/expires, DHCP enabled.

Why it works:
DHCP issues often involve options (gateway/DNS), not just the IP address.

Success indicates:
All expected fields present and consistent with the site standard.

Failure indicates:
Missing/incorrect gateway/DNS, unexpected DHCP Server, DHCP disabled, or odd lease timing.

Common pitfall:
Using `ipconfig` short output and missing DHCP Server/lease details.

column1:
User has a valid IP (not 169.254) but cannot reach the internet. What should you check FIRST?

A. Default gateway reachability
B. DNS records
C. Antivirus
D. Browser cache
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <default-gateway>

What it checks:
Whether the default gateway is present, correct, and reachable.

Why it works:
Without a reachable gateway, off-subnet routing fails regardless of DNS.

Success indicates:
Gateway ping succeeds and gateway matches expected subnet design.

Failure indicates:
Gateway missing/wrong/unreachable → wrong scope option, wrong VLAN/port, or L2 issue.

Common pitfall:
Starting with DNS when routing is broken.

column1:
User can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot reach google.com by name. In DHCP terms, what is MOST likely wrong?

A. Wrong gateway
B. Wrong DNS servers handed out
C. Lease expired
D. VLAN mismatch
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping 8.8.8.8
ping google.com

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers are present/correct when IP routing works.

Why it works:
DHCP distributes DNS servers; wrong DNS yields IP reachability but name failure.

Success indicates:
DNS servers corrected and names resolve after renew.

Failure indicates:
Names still fail; DNS servers missing/incorrect in ipconfig /all.

Common pitfall:
Blaming the ISP when it’s a DNS option issue.

column1:
ipconfig /all shows Default Gateway is blank. What does that MOST likely indicate?

A. DNS cache stale
B. DHCP scope option for gateway missing/misconfigured
C. Malware
D. Subnet mask too small
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Whether a gateway was provided and whether off-subnet routing is possible.

Why it works:
Without a gateway, the client can only talk to its local subnet.

Success indicates:
Gateway appears correctly after renew and off-subnet ping succeeds.

Failure indicates:
Gateway stays blank and off-subnet pings fail, indicating DHCP option issue or static config.

Common pitfall:
Focusing on DNS when the gateway is missing.

column1:
Some users work; new devices get 169.254.x.x. What is a likely cause?

A. DHCP scope exhaustion
B. DNS poisoning
C. Proxy settings
D. Corrupt profile
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (new device)
ipconfig /all (existing device)

What it checks:
Whether new devices fail to obtain leases while existing leases remain valid.

Why it works:
Scope exhaustion blocks new leases but doesn’t immediately break existing ones.

Success indicates:
After scope expansion/freeing addresses, new devices obtain valid leases.

Failure indicates:
New devices remain APIPA; existing devices still work.

Common pitfall:
Assuming it’s cabling without recognizing the 'new devices only' pattern.

column1:
User receives an IP in an unexpected range (192.168.1.x instead of 10.20.30.x). What is MOST likely?

A. Windows picked a random IP
B. Wrong DHCP server (rogue) or wrong VLAN/SSID
C. Missing DNS suffix
D. Browser misconfig
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
DHCP Server field and whether the IP range matches expected network design.

Why it works:
Wrong DHCP source or VLAN/SSID mapping can hand out an entirely different scope.

Success indicates:
DHCP Server matches expected and IP range matches the intended subnet.

Failure indicates:
Unexpected DHCP Server (e.g., home router/hotspot) or IP range matches guest network.

Common pitfall:
Not checking the DHCP Server field and guessing based only on the IP range.

column1:
Connectivity breaks when a user moves desks; sometimes they get APIPA. What should you suspect?

A. Laptop defect
B. Switch port/VLAN configuration differs between desks
C. DNS caching
D. Password policy
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (after move)
Compare with a working desk

What it checks:
Whether failures correlate with physical port/location and whether IP range changes.

Why it works:
Different ports can be mapped to different VLANs; a misconfigured port may lack DHCP/relay.

Success indicates:
User receives valid lease consistently at all desks after port/VLAN fix.

Failure indicates:
APIPA or wrong IP range occurs only at certain desks.

Common pitfall:
Replacing hardware before correlating to location.

column1:
User has valid IP and can ping gateway, but internal servers by name fail. Which DHCP-delivered setting is most likely wrong?

A. Subnet mask
B. DNS servers
C. Default gateway
D. Lease duration
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup <internal-hostname>

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers are correct for internal name resolution.

Why it works:
Routing is OK (gateway ping works); name failures point to DNS misconfiguration distributed via DHCP.

Success indicates:
nslookup resolves internal hostnames using expected DNS servers.

Failure indicates:
nslookup fails or uses wrong DNS servers; internal names do not resolve.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS server outage instead of checking DHCP-delivered DNS values.

column1:
User can reach internet sites but not internal hostnames. What is a common DHCP cause in hybrid MSP environments?

A. DHCP handed out public DNS only (missing internal DNS)
B. Wrong subnet mask
C. NIC failing
D. Windows update pending
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalhost
nslookup google.com

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers include internal resolvers for internal zones.

Why it works:
Public DNS resolves internet names but cannot resolve internal zones; DHCP may need to supply internal DNS (split DNS).

Success indicates:
Internal hostnames resolve once internal DNS is assigned.

Failure indicates:
Internal hostnames fail while external names work.

Common pitfall:
Assuming 'internet works' means DNS is correct for internal services.

column1:
User has correct-looking IP and gateway, but off-subnet traffic still fails. Which DHCP field should you double-check next?

A. Lease expires
B. Subnet mask
C. Host name
D. Physical address
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Subnet mask correctness and whether it matches the expected design for that VLAN.

Why it works:
Wrong subnet mask causes incorrect routing decisions (treating remote as local or vice versa).

Success indicates:
Mask corrected and connectivity stabilizes after renew.

Failure indicates:
Off-subnet still fails; mask is wrong or VLAN is incorrect.

Common pitfall:
Ignoring the subnet mask because the IP and gateway 'look right'.

column1:
Best sequence to force a client to pick up updated DHCP options after scope changes?

A. ipconfig /flushdns then ipconfig /displaydns
B. ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
C. ping 8.8.8.8 then ping google.com
D. nslookup then set type=SRV
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Forces a new DHCP request and validates updated options (gateway/DNS).

Why it works:
DHCP options are delivered at lease negotiation; releasing/renewing fetches new values.

Success indicates:
Lease shows updated DNS/gateway and connectivity improves.

Failure indicates:
Options remain unchanged or renew fails, indicating server-side scope still wrong or wrong DHCP source.

Common pitfall:
Renewing without validating changes in ipconfig /all.

column1:
On the same network, one machine shows DHCP Server 10.0.0.5 and another shows 192.168.1.1. What does that MOST likely indicate?

A. Normal behavior
B. Multiple DHCP servers (possibly rogue) handing out leases
C. DNS is down
D. User account locked
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (both machines)

What it checks:
Inconsistent DHCP Server values and differing options/ranges.

Why it works:
Multiple DHCP servers cause inconsistent configuration and intermittent failures.

Success indicates:
All clients show the same expected DHCP Server and consistent options.

Failure indicates:
Different DHCP servers appear; clients get different IP ranges/options.

Common pitfall:
Focusing on apps/DNS before proving the DHCP source inconsistency.

column1:
User’s ipconfig /all shows the correct DNS and gateway, but internal apps still fail. What should you check NEXT?

A. Confirm DNS resolution of internal names
B. Reset password
C. Disable firewall
D. Replace switch
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
nslookup internalhost
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether internal name resolution is functioning with the configured DNS servers.

Why it works:
With a reachable gateway and correct options, name resolution is a common remaining dependency.

Success indicates:
nslookup returns correct internal IPs and app connectivity returns.

Failure indicates:
nslookup fails or resolves incorrectly; points to DNS/server-side issue or wrong resolvers.

Common pitfall:
Assuming gateway ping equals full access.

column1:
Connectivity drops every few minutes and then returns. Which DHCP-related factor could contribute?

A. Very short lease time or renew failures
B. DNS TTL
C. Browser cache
D. Keyboard driver
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (check Lease Obtained/Expires)
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Lease timing and whether renewals are successful.

Why it works:
Short leases or renew failures can cause periodic loss of connectivity.

Success indicates:
Lease duration is normal; renew succeeds; drops stop after fix.

Failure indicates:
Lease expires quickly or renew fails around the time drops occur.

Common pitfall:
Assuming all intermittent drops are Wi‑Fi signal issues without checking leases.

column1:
User is on the office network but receives a guest-network IP range. What is MOST likely?

A. Malware changed settings
B. Wrong VLAN/SSID mapping or wrong switch port config
C. DNS cache issue
D. Outlook profile issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare IP range/DHCP Server to expected

What it checks:
Whether the client is placed into a guest segment (different scope).

Why it works:
Segmentation maps ports/SSIDs to VLANs and DHCP scopes; misplacement yields wrong scope.

Success indicates:
Client receives correct corporate IP range and reaches internal resources.

Failure indicates:
Client stays in guest range; DHCP Server appears as guest gateway/router.

Common pitfall:
Troubleshooting applications before confirming network placement.

column1:
Which ipconfig /all field most directly identifies which device issued the DHCP lease?

A. DNS Servers
B. DHCP Server
C. Subnet Mask
D. Node Type
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
The DHCP Server field shows the server that granted the lease.

Why it works:
This is crucial for detecting rogue DHCP and validating expected design.

Success indicates:
DHCP Server matches known-good client/environment.

Failure indicates:
Unexpected DHCP Server indicates wrong VLAN/SSID or rogue DHCP.

Common pitfall:
Looking only at the IP range and missing the DHCP Server field.

column1:
User gets APIPA on wired but works on Wi‑Fi. Best next check?

A. Compare ipconfig /all between wired and Wi‑Fi
B. Flush DNS
C. Reset password
D. Reinstall Windows
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (wired)
ipconfig /all (Wi‑Fi)

What it checks:
Whether DHCP succeeds on Wi‑Fi but fails on wired and whether options/DHCP server differ.

Why it works:
If Wi‑Fi works, the OS stack is fine; wired path points to port/VLAN/cable issues.

Success indicates:
Wired obtains valid lease like Wi‑Fi and connectivity returns.

Failure indicates:
Wired remains APIPA or shows wrong DHCP server/range.

Common pitfall:
Replacing hardware before validating port/VLAN differences.

column1:
Client has valid IP but cannot reach internal servers by IP or name. Gateway ping fails. What category of issue is most likely FIRST?

A. DNS
B. Gateway/VLAN/Layer 2 connectivity
C. User permissions
D. Browser cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Whether the gateway is reachable; required for routing to other subnets.

Why it works:
If gateway is unreachable, routing/L2/VLAN is the first suspect, not DNS.

Success indicates:
Gateway ping succeeds; then proceed to DNS tests if names fail.

Failure indicates:
Gateway ping fails; wrong VLAN/port, wrong gateway option, or L2 issue.

Common pitfall:
Spending time on DNS when the gateway is unreachable.

column1:
Why can DHCP issues look like DNS issues?

A. DHCP resolves names
B. DHCP distributes DNS server addresses to clients
C. DNS assigns IPs
D. DNS controls gateways
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping 8.8.8.8
ping google.com

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers were handed out correctly and whether IP works without names.

Why it works:
Wrong DNS via DHCP yields IP reachability but name resolution failure.

Success indicates:
Correct DNS listed and name resolution works.

Failure indicates:
Incorrect/missing DNS listed; names fail while IP works.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS server outage instead of checking DHCP-delivered DNS servers.

column1:
After server-side DHCP option fixes, what is the best client-side step to pick up new options?

A. ipconfig /displaydns
B. ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
C. ping google.com
D. Restart Outlook
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Forces a new lease request and verifies the updated options are applied.

Why it works:
DHCP options are delivered during lease negotiation; renew fetches them.

Success indicates:
ipconfig /all shows corrected DNS/gateway and connectivity improves.

Failure indicates:
Options remain wrong or renew fails; scope still wrong or wrong DHCP source.

Common pitfall:
Only flushing DNS cache without correcting the configured DNS servers.

column1:
You suspect DHCP handed out wrong DNS. Which quick test supports that?

A. ping 8.8.8.8 works but internal hostname lookup fails
B. ping gateway fails
C. ipconfig shows APIPA
D. Keyboard stops working
column2:
Correct Answer: A

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalhost
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Whether IP routing works and internal name resolution fails with the configured DNS servers.

Why it works:
IP works but internal name fails strongly suggests DNS configuration (often via DHCP options).

Success indicates:
After correcting DNS servers and renewing, internalhost resolves.

Failure indicates:
Internalhost still fails; DNS servers are wrong or internal DNS unreachable.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS is fine because internet sites resolve.

column1:
In MSP environments, DHCP may run on a firewall instead of Windows Server. What is the correct approach when you see the firewall listed as DHCP Server?

A. Assume it’s wrong and change it
B. Validate against known-good client/design for that customer
C. Reinstall the NIC
D. Flush DNS cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with known-good machine or documentation

What it checks:
Whether the DHCP source matches the intended design for that client.

Why it works:
Client setups vary; validating prevents misdiagnosing a legitimate configuration.

Success indicates:
DHCP Server matches expected design and options are correct.

Failure indicates:
DHCP Server differs from known-good and options/range are wrong.

Common pitfall:
Assuming one 'standard' DHCP design across all clients.

column1:
A user can access internal resources by IP but not hostname. Which DHCP-delivered setting is likely wrong?

A. Default gateway
B. DNS servers
C. Lease duration
D. DHCP Enabled
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalhost
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
DNS server addresses and name resolution behavior.

Why it works:
IP bypasses DNS; hostnames require DNS, commonly delivered via DHCP.

Success indicates:
Internal names resolve after correcting DNS servers and renewing.

Failure indicates:
Names fail; DNS servers wrong/missing or public-only.

Common pitfall:
Blaming routing when IP connectivity already works.

column1:
User has two DNS servers: one internal, one public. Internal names fail intermittently. What’s likely happening?

A. Gateway is down
B. Client queries public DNS sometimes
C. Lease expired
D. APIPA
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalhost (repeat)

What it checks:
Configured resolvers and inconsistent resolution behavior.

Why it works:
Public DNS cannot resolve internal zones; mixed resolvers cause intermittent failures.

Success indicates:
After removing public DNS from DHCP options, internal resolution stabilizes.

Failure indicates:
Internal lookups sometimes fail; behavior correlates with resolver used.

Common pitfall:
Treating intermittent DNS as random rather than configuration-driven.

column1:
User renews DHCP and still has wrong DNS. Most likely reason?

A. Renew can’t change options
B. Scope/options not fixed or wrong DHCP source
C. NIC failing
D. Browser cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether options changed and which DHCP server supplied them.

Why it works:
If server-side options aren’t corrected (or rogue DHCP), renew repeats wrong values.

Success indicates:
After fixing scope and renewing, DNS becomes correct.

Failure indicates:
DNS remains wrong; scope still misconfigured or wrong DHCP server issuing lease.

Common pitfall:
Only flushing DNS cache.

column1:
Only one conference room causes APIPA; elsewhere works. Best interpretation?

A. Laptop defect
B. Port/VLAN lacks DHCP/relay or misconfigured
C. DNS down
D. Password wrong
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with another port

What it checks:
Location-specific DHCP behavior and IP range differences.

Why it works:
Location-specific failures indicate port/VLAN/relay issues, not OS.

Success indicates:
After port/VLAN fix, valid lease obtained in that room.

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists only in that room.

Common pitfall:
Replacing laptop before confirming location correlation.

column1:
User has valid IP, gateway reachable, but no internet by IP or name for everyone on that network. First suspect?

A. Browser issue
B. Upstream firewall/ISP/routing issue
C. Scope exhaustion
D. DNS cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
ping 8.8.8.8
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether local gateway works but upstream connectivity fails broadly.

Why it works:
Correct local lease + broad upstream failure points beyond DHCP to firewall/ISP/routing.

Success indicates:
Upstream restored; clients work without changing leases.

Failure indicates:
Gateway works but upstream ping fails for many users.

Common pitfall:
Rebuilding leases when the outage is upstream.

column1:
Which symptom best indicates wrong gateway handed out by DHCP?

A. IP ping works but name fails
B. Gateway ping fails and off-subnet fails
C. nslookup NXDOMAIN
D. APIPA
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Gateway presence/correctness and ability to route.

Why it works:
Wrong/unreachable gateway prevents routing, breaking off-subnet traffic.

Success indicates:
Gateway ping succeeds; off-subnet pings succeed.

Failure indicates:
Gateway ping fails; off-subnet fails.

Common pitfall:
Mislabeling as DNS.

column1:
Client gets correct IP range but wrong subnet mask. Likely impact?

A. Only DNS breaks
B. Intermittent/broken routing decisions
C. Always APIPA
D. Browser cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Subnet mask value vs expected.

Why it works:
Wrong mask changes what the client treats as local vs routed.

Success indicates:
After correcting mask via DHCP options, connectivity stabilizes.

Failure indicates:
Connectivity remains inconsistent; mask still wrong.

Common pitfall:
Skipping mask review.

column1:
Internet works but internal servers do not. Suspect public DNS only. Best verification?

A. Ping internal IP
B. Verify DNS servers + nslookup internalhost
C. Flush DNS only
D. Reset router
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalhost

What it checks:
Configured DNS servers and internal name resolution.

Why it works:
Public DNS can’t resolve internal zones; verifying confirms misconfiguration.

Success indicates:
Internal names resolve after internal DNS is provided and lease renewed.

Failure indicates:
Internal names fail; DNS servers are public-only.

Common pitfall:
Flushing cache without fixing resolver addresses.

column1:
Devices intermittently receive wrong IP ranges. Best evidence to escalate?

A. Browser screenshot
B. ipconfig /all showing unexpected DHCP Server + IP range
C. List of usernames
D. Windows build number
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Lease source (DHCP Server) and actual lease values.

Why it works:
Provides concrete proof of rogue DHCP or wrong VLAN mapping.

Success indicates:
DHCP Server matches expected; IP range correct.

Failure indicates:
Unexpected DHCP Server and wrong range shown.

Common pitfall:
Escalating without hard evidence.

column1:
User can ping gateway but cannot ping 8.8.8.8. DNS irrelevant yet. What does that suggest?

A. DNS issue
B. Upstream routing/firewall issue beyond gateway
C. Scope exhaustion
D. APIPA
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
ping 8.8.8.8
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Local L2 to gateway vs upstream routing.

Why it works:
If gateway reachable but upstream not, issue is beyond local client config.

Success indicates:
Upstream ping succeeds after network fix; no lease change needed.

Failure indicates:
Upstream ping fails for many clients; points to firewall/ISP.

Common pitfall:
Chasing DNS before confirming IP routing.

column1:
User has APIPA but only on one switch. Elsewhere OK. Best next move?

A. Release/renew repeatedly
B. Compare with known-good port and escalate VLAN/relay issue
C. Flush DNS
D. Reinstall Windows
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare another port/area

What it checks:
Whether the issue is tied to a specific switch/IDF or port group.

Why it works:
Location-tied APIPA suggests VLAN/relay/port config issue.

Success indicates:
Valid lease on corrected port; APIPA gone.

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists on that switch/ports.

Common pitfall:
Treating as a client OS issue.

column1:
What is the best first command when a user says 'I got moved to a new office and now nothing works'?

A. nslookup
B. ipconfig /all
C. ipconfig /flushdns
D. whoami
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Confirms DHCP lease details, gateway, DNS, and DHCP Server to detect wrong VLAN/scope.

Why it works:
Desk moves often involve port/VLAN changes; ipconfig /all surfaces it immediately.

Success indicates:
Lease matches expected for that location and network works.

Failure indicates:
IP range/gateway/DNS/DHCP Server differ from expected; indicates wrong port/VLAN.

Common pitfall:
Starting with DNS before validating the lease.

column1:
User says 'I can reach google.com but not internal share by hostname'. Best DHCP-related suspicion?

A. Wrong gateway
B. Missing internal DNS / split DNS issue
C. Lease expired
D. APIPA
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internalshare
ping <internal-share-ip>

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers include internal resolvers for internal zones.

Why it works:
External resolution can work with public DNS while internal zones require internal DNS.

Success indicates:
Internal share resolves after correct internal DNS is assigned.

Failure indicates:
Internal hostname fails; DNS servers are public-only.

Common pitfall:
Assuming the file server is down.

column1:
User’s IP is valid but DHCP Server field is blank. What’s most likely?

A. DNS server outage
B. Static IP configuration (DHCP not used)
C. Scope exhaustion
D. VLAN mismatch
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether DHCP is enabled and whether a DHCP server issued the lease.

Why it works:
If the system is static, there may be no DHCP Server listed.

Success indicates:
Switching to DHCP obtains lease and DHCP Server appears.

Failure indicates:
DHCP is disabled or static config is wrong.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP server is down when the client is static.

column1:
User receives correct IP but DNS Servers list is empty. What does that indicate?

A. Normal; DNS auto-detects
B. DHCP scope options missing DNS servers
C. APIPA
D. ISP outage
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping 8.8.8.8
ping google.com

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers were provided and whether name resolution works.

Why it works:
No DNS servers means name resolution will fail even if routing works.

Success indicates:
DNS servers appear after renew and names resolve.

Failure indicates:
DNS servers remain empty; names fail.

Common pitfall:
Flushing DNS cache instead of providing DNS servers.

column1:
Some users work; others get valid IP but wrong gateway. Best guess?

A. Random Windows bug
B. Multiple scopes or misconfigured option on one VLAN/SSID
C. DNS poisoning
D. Password lockout
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (working)
ipconfig /all (failing)
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Whether gateway differs by VLAN/SSID/port and whether it’s reachable.

Why it works:
A misconfigured scope option can hand out wrong gateway causing no routing.

Success indicates:
Gateway matches expected and reachable after fix.

Failure indicates:
Gateway differs/unreachable on failing clients.

Common pitfall:
Assuming all 'valid IPs' are equal.

column1:
User gets APIPA after docking/undocking. Wi‑Fi works. What is the best check?

A. Browser cache
B. Compare adapter configs; wired may be disabled or wrong VLAN
C. Reset password
D. Reinstall OS
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Ethernet)
ipconfig /all (Wi‑Fi)

What it checks:
Whether Ethernet adapter is DHCP enabled and obtaining a lease when docked.

Why it works:
Dock/Ethernet path can have port/VLAN/cable issues independent of Wi‑Fi.

Success indicates:
Ethernet obtains valid lease and works when docked.

Failure indicates:
Ethernet stays APIPA; Wi‑Fi ok; points to dock/cable/port/VLAN.

Common pitfall:
Blaming Wi‑Fi when the failing path is Ethernet.

column1:
A user can reach internal servers on the same subnet but not other subnets. Gateway ping works. Best next check?

A. DNS only
B. Check if correct gateway and routes exist; then test off-subnet IPs
C. Reinstall OS
D. Flush DNS
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>
ping <known-offsubnet-ip>

What it checks:
Whether off-subnet routing works and whether the gateway is correct for inter-VLAN routing.

Why it works:
Gateway may be reachable but not routing to other subnets due to upstream rules; validate with off-subnet IP tests.

Success indicates:
Off-subnet IP pings succeed after upstream routing/firewall fix.

Failure indicates:
Off-subnet IP pings fail; indicates upstream routing/firewall.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP is still the issue when lease is correct.

column1:
User receives valid IP but can’t access internal sites over VPN; internet works. DHCP on VPN isn’t used—what’s still relevant?

A. Nothing
B. DNS settings pushed by VPN can resemble DHCP option issues
C. Only subnet mask
D. Only lease time
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (after VPN)
nslookup internalhost

What it checks:
Whether DNS servers changed when VPN connected and if internal names resolve.

Why it works:
VPN 'options' behave like DHCP options; wrong DNS on VPN breaks internal names.

Success indicates:
Internal names resolve with VPN DNS.

Failure indicates:
Internal names fail; VPN DNS wrong/missing.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP is irrelevant because VPN is involved.

column1:
User’s gateway is correct but ARP/neighbor issues suspected; what client-side signal suggests L2/port problem rather than DHCP?

A. APIPA
B. Gateway ping fails despite correct lease
C. google.com fails to resolve
D. Lease expires tomorrow
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether the client can reach the gateway at L2.

Why it works:
DHCP can succeed but L2 issues can still block traffic; gateway reachability is a reality check.

Success indicates:
Gateway ping succeeds; proceed to DNS/upstream tests.

Failure indicates:
Gateway ping fails; points to L2/port/VLAN issues.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP success guarantees L2 health.

column1:
A user says 'I only lose access to internal resources, internet is fine'. DHCP delivered DNS is correct. What next?

A. Reinstall OS
B. Compare with known-good; suspect VLAN ACLs or upstream rules
C. Flush DNS
D. Renew lease repeatedly
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Whether internal routing is blocked even with correct lease settings.

Why it works:
Correct DHCP settings with selective internal failure points upstream (ACLs/firewall).

Success indicates:
Internal IP pings succeed after ACL fix; no lease change needed.

Failure indicates:
Internal IP pings fail while internet works; upstream restriction.

Common pitfall:
Over-rotating on DHCP when it’s an upstream policy issue.

column1:
You run ipconfig /all and see 'DHCP Enabled: Yes' but the client has a static IP configured elsewhere. What is the most practical interpretation?

A. DHCP is broken
B. The client may be using a static IP despite DHCP enabled status showing Yes on another adapter
C. DNS issue
D. Scope exhaustion
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Adapter-by-adapter settings; multiple adapters may show different DHCP states.

Why it works:
Multiple adapters (Ethernet/Wi‑Fi/virtual) can differ; the active adapter may be static/misconfigured.

Success indicates:
Active adapter shows correct DHCP lease and connectivity works.

Failure indicates:
Active adapter is static/wrong; lease is on an inactive adapter.

Common pitfall:
Reading ipconfig /all without identifying the active adapter.

column1:
A user’s device works until they connect to a particular docking station, then they get a wrong IP range. Best hypothesis?

A. Dock is infected
B. Dock port is patched to a different VLAN/SSID/port profile
C. DNS cache
D. Lease duration
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (docked)
ipconfig /all (undocked)

What it checks:
IP range and DHCP Server differences by connection method.

Why it works:
Different physical connections can map to different VLANs/scopes.

Success indicates:
Docked connection gets the correct range after port/VLAN correction.

Failure indicates:
Docked connection repeatedly gets wrong range; DHCP Server differs.

Common pitfall:
Assuming docks are purely 'hardware' and ignoring network mapping.
